W09.concept: A data parser does more than recognise punctuation. Some formats can request external data or expand complex structures, so configure the parser for the feature you actually need.
W09.mechanism: Accept only the document capabilities the feature needs. Control external resolution, expansion and resource use, then validate the parsed values.
W09.example: For a harmless local parser exercise, accept a fixed small record structure. Test a normal record, unexpected fields, oversized nesting, and a document containing a declaration that your safe configuration should reject. Confirm the parser makes no unexpected resource access using the provider's controlled lab, rather than relying only on the displayed error.
W09.pitfall: XML schema validation and external-entity configuration solve different problems. Do not assume enabling one disables the other.

check.question: Which capability should an untrusted XML parser usually avoid unless explicitly required?
choices: Resolving external entities through filesystem or network access
Reading ordinary permitted element text
Reporting malformed syntax
check.explanation: External resolution introduces additional resource and trust boundaries beyond the submitted document.

guide.bridge: You know URLs, network routes and server APIs. Use the supplied fictional fetch-service diagram and authorised lab.
guide.teaching:
### Follow whose network access is used

A browser requesting a URL uses the browser's network position. A server fetching that URL uses the server's position and permissions. It may reach internal services unavailable to the user.

A preview, import or image-fetching feature can therefore become an unintended bridge into a private network. The important question is which destinations the feature is meant to reach.

### Define allowed destinations

Prefer a small trusted destination set when the feature permits it. Parse URLs with an appropriate parser, allow only required schemes and restrict the final destination. Check address resolution, redirects and alternate address forms under the actual client library.

Validating one hostname string is insufficient if later resolution or a redirect sends the request somewhere else. A change between checking a name and using it is another timing problem to consider.

### Limit what a fetch can do

Use network restrictions, limited credentials, timeouts and response-size limits. Prevent the fetch worker from inheriting broad internal access simply because it runs on a server.

### Check the final connection

For each harmless lab case, record the requested URL, redirects, resolved destination and allowed outcome. A blocked spelling of one private address does not establish that the destination policy holds for every route.
guide.example:
Synthetic allowlist: https://docs.example on port 443, no redirects
A: https://docs.example/help       -> allow
B: https://docs.example.evil.example/help -> deny
C: http://docs.example/help        -> deny scheme
D: https://docs.example:444/help    -> deny port
E: allowed A redirects elsewhere   -> reject redirect under this policy
guide.explanation: The host in B is the longer name ending evil.example, not docs.example. Parsing separates scheme, authority and path; string containment does not. This fixture assumes destination resolution is also constrained by a separate egress policy, which must be verified in a real deployment.
guide.exercise: Classify all five supplied cases and add https://other.example/docs.example as a sixth. Explain which component of each URL determines the allowlist comparison.
guide.solution: Only A is allowed; the sixth is denied because its host is other.example. A path containing an allowed name does not change the destination authority.
guide.challenge: Design a link-preview service supporting only two fixed documentation hosts. State redirect, timeout, size, credential and egress policies. Give a negative case for each boundary without making network requests.
guide.challenge_solution: One paper design allows only HTTPS on port 443 for docs.example and help.example, no redirects, no forwarded user cookies or authorisation headers, a 3-second total request deadline and a 1 MB response cap. A separately enforced egress policy restricts actual destinations, including after DNS resolution, and blocks internal-only services. Negative cases: another hostname, port 444, a redirect even from an allowed host, an oversize response, a deadline overrun, or attempted credential forwarding all fail closed. These illustrative limits are policy choices, not universal production settings. No network request is needed to evaluate the cases.

W10.concept: A server may fetch a web address for a user. Server-side request forgery occurs when that user can make the server reach destinations it should not access.
W10.mechanism: Control the actual destinations the server can reach, including redirects and resolution. Limit the fetcher's network authority and resource use.
W10.example: Design a local thumbnail service that accepts IDs for a fixed image catalogue instead of free-form URLs. For the linked lab, record the server's network position and which boundary the unintended request crosses. Compare initial destination validation with redirect handling and explain why checking only the visible input string is incomplete.
W10.pitfall: An apparently public hostname can resolve differently over time. Destination policy must consider the address actually used and subsequent hops.

check.question: Why is SSRF dangerous even when the response is not returned to the caller?
choices: A hidden response guarantees no effect occurred
The server may still perform an unintended action or reach a protected service
Only browser-origin rules determine server-side access
check.explanation: The request itself may have side effects or cross a network trust boundary, regardless of response visibility.

guide.bridge: B03 introduced API contracts and S06 introduced object permissions. Use fictional accounts and objects in the training API.
guide.teaching:
### Read the documented operation

An endpoint contract states its method, fields and responses. Identify which fields choose an object and which fields ask to change it. Documentation helps explain intent; server behaviour determines what is actually enforced.

### Check the selected object

If user A requests object 2, resolve A from the trusted session and check permission on object 2. An unpredictable object identifier can reduce guessing but is not an ownership rule. List and search endpoints need the same care as a single-object route.

### Choose writable fields explicitly

A request may include an unexpected owner_id or admin field. Passing every supplied field directly into an update can let a caller change protected properties. Define the allowed input fields for each operation rather than assuming a visible form is the only client.

### Bound queries and results

Validate types, lengths and ranges. Set page-size and resource limits, and decide how unknown fields are handled. A request that follows JSON syntax may still demand excessive work.

Compare permitted and denied operations with two fictional users. Check the stored state after each attempted write, not only the response text.
guide.example:
Objects: n1={owner:A,body:"one"}; n2={owner:B,body:"two"}
PATCH /notes/{id}: body field only; max 100 chars
A PATCH n1 {body:"new"} -> allow
A PATCH n2 {body:"new"} -> deny ownership
A PATCH n1 {owner:"B"}  -> reject protected field
A PATCH n1 {body:7}     -> reject type
No identity PATCH n1   -> deny authentication
guide.explanation: The ownership decision uses the stored object and authenticated principal. Rejecting an owner field prevents the request from changing the very state used to authorise it. The policy can consistently reject all unknown keys rather than silently accepting misspellings.
guide.exercise: Build the five-case test matrix in Learn and add B reading n2, B reading n1 and A updating a 101-character body. Identify whether each failure is authentication, object access or schema validation.
guide.solution: A PATCH n1 with a string body is allowed. A PATCH n2 fails object access. A supplying owner fails the writable-field schema. A supplying body 7 fails type validation. No-identity PATCH fails authentication. Added cases: B reading n2 is allowed; B reading n1 fails object access; A updating n1 with 101 characters fails the 100-character limit. Check both returned response and stored object: denied cases must leave it unchanged.
guide.challenge: Add an internal audit_only field that ordinary users cannot read. Define response fields and update fields separately, then describe how you would test that a normal GET does not expose audit_only.
guide.challenge_solution: One policy returns only id and body on ordinary GET; owner may be used internally without being returned, and audit_only is never included. The PATCH writable allowlist contains only body. Given n1 with audit_only="internal-demo", test that A’s GET includes the expected body but no audit_only key, that A cannot PATCH audit_only, and that B cannot GET n1 at all. Inspect the raw JSON response as well as the visible UI; hiding a received field does not protect it.

W11.concept: An API should accept only the operations and fields a user is allowed to control. A valid request shape does not prove access to the object it names.
W11.mechanism: Validate the operation, check access to each selected object and allow only intended writable fields. Apply limits to queries as well as individual records.
W11.example: Create two synthetic accounts and one private note per account. Build a test matrix for read, update, and delete using each identity and each note ID. Add an unexpected owner_id field to a local update request and ensure the server does not silently reassign ownership. Record the expected result for every row before running the tests.
W11.pitfall: API documentation describes intended behaviour; it does not enforce it. The implementation must reject forbidden combinations.

check.question: What should happen when a valid user supplies another user's private object ID?
choices: The ID's existence automatically grants access
The browser decides whether the database should return it
The server applies object-level permission checks and denies unauthorised access
check.explanation: The server must evaluate the actor-object-action relationship on every relevant operation.

guide.bridge: S06 separated identity from permission. Here you will inspect a fictional account flow without attempting real sign-ins.
guide.teaching:
### Map every entry route

List sign-in, password reset, recovery, remembered devices and any federation provider. An attacker may choose the weakest route. A strong password check does not help if recovery can transfer the account with weaker evidence.

### Avoid revealing unnecessary account information

Enumeration means discovering which accounts exist. Different messages, timings or response codes can disclose that information. Choose a response policy that balances privacy with useful recovery guidance, and test more than the displayed sentence.

### Protect recovery credentials

A reset token should have suitable unpredictability, lifetime and use restrictions. Bind it to the intended account and operation. Check what happens when a password changes or a token is reused.

Rate limits and abuse monitoring help constrain repeated guesses and message floods. Do not lock out legitimate users casually or rely on one IP address as the only identity.

### Recheck session handling

After successful sign-in or a privilege change, manage session identifiers appropriately. On logout or account restriction, document which sessions stop working and how soon. A button saying “signed out” is not proof that a previously issued credential is unusable.
guide.example:
Fictional reset state
Token R1: account A, purpose password-reset, expires at 12:00, unused
11:59 R1 + valid new password -> accept, mark used
11:59 R1 second submission     -> reject used
12:01 fresh unused R1 scenario -> reject expired
R1 used as login session      -> reject wrong purpose
guide.explanation: The second row follows the first, while the expired row is a separate fresh-state scenario. Keeping those sequences explicit prevents impossible test expectations. Token validation and consumption should be atomic enough that concurrent attempts cannot both succeed.
guide.exercise: Trace the four supplied cases. Add a token for account B submitted to reset A, and a request with no token. State what must be checked and what a generic public response should avoid disclosing.
guide.solution: Bind account/purpose, check expiry and unused state, then consume deliberately. Foreign-account and absent tokens reject. Public messages should avoid unnecessary account-existence disclosure; internal logs can retain safe reason codes.
guide.challenge: Draw reset-request, issued, consumed and expired states. Give one concurrent-use test and one verification that a reset token cannot be used as an ordinary session credential.
guide.challenge_solution: Paper transitions: request → issued/unused after approved generation; issued/unused → consumed after valid account/purpose/time checks and atomic redemption; issued/unused → expired at the deadline. Consumed and expired tokens cannot return to unused; a new request issues a different token. Concurrent case: two redemptions of the same unused token reach the protected consume step; at most one succeeds and the other sees consumed. Purpose case: submit the reset token to the ordinary session validator and expect rejection even before considering object access. Document whether a real password reset revokes old sessions; do not assume it does.

W12.concept: Signing in, resetting a password and recovering an account are all ways into that account. Protect the whole journey rather than only the main password form.
W12.mechanism: Review sign-in and recovery as one system. Protect tokens, limit abuse, control account disclosures and verify what happens to existing sessions.
W12.example: Draw a test account's normal login and lost-password paths. For a local recovery flow, test an expired token, a reused token, and a token presented for the wrong account. Confirm that a successful reset changes the intended credential and follows the application's session-revocation policy. Use only synthetic accounts in the training environment.
W12.pitfall: A recovery message can be generic while other observable differences still reveal account existence. Examine the complete behaviour.

check.question: Which path deserves the same security attention as normal login?
choices: Password and multifactor recovery
Only the public colour-theme switch
Only the site's logo download
check.explanation: Recovery can confer account access, so its authority and abuse resistance are part of authentication security.

guide.bridge: S06 introduced authorisation. Use two fictional users and a small table of notes, invoices or bookings.
guide.teaching:
### Write the rule in a sentence

For example: “A customer may read their own invoice, but may not change its paid amount.” That identifies a person, action, object and condition. “The invoice page is secure” does not.

Turn the sentence into allowed and denied cases. Include another customer's object and an account without a session.

### Check every route to the action

A page, an API, a download route and a batch operation may reach the same underlying data. Protect each relevant path. Complete mediation means checking access wherever an operation needs it, not only at the first screen.

### Respect the workflow

An action can be allowed in one state and denied in another. Editing a draft differs from changing an issued invoice. Validate current state on the server at the moment the action is applied.

### Test effects, not appearances

Hiding a control or returning an error is not enough if the stored data still changes. Inspect the authorised lab's before-and-after state. Also check that a permitted action still succeeds; a feature that denies everyone is not a correct access policy.

Keep object identifiers separate from proof of ownership. An obscure URL may still be shared or leaked.
guide.example:
Policy: owner edits draft invoice only; reviewer approves; no one edits approved totals.
I1: owner A, draft, total 100
I2: owner B, approved, total 200
A edit I1 -> yes
A edit I2 -> no
B edit I2 -> no (state)
Reviewer approve I1 -> yes
Reviewer edit approved I2 -> no
guide.explanation: B owns I2 but the approved-state invariant still denies editing. A reviewer role grants approval, not arbitrary alteration. These distinctions should be visible in the tests rather than encoded as “admin can do everything.”
guide.exercise: Evaluate the five supplied cases and add an unauthenticated edit, an owner edit after concurrent approval and a bulk-edit endpoint containing I1/I2. State an explicit partial-versus-atomic bulk policy.
guide.solution: The original five decisions are allow, deny, deny, allow, deny. No-identity edit is denied. If approval commits before the owner’s edit, the edit must see approved state and fail. For the bulk example choose all-or-nothing: A submits changes to I1 and I2; I2 fails owner/state checks, so neither change commits, including I1. A per-item-results policy could also be valid, but it must report each decision and preserve every item’s rules.
guide.challenge: Propose server checks and transaction boundaries for approve-and-lock. Give a test where two requests race, and explain why checking only the initial page-load state is insufficient.
guide.challenge_solution: Example paper schedule: editor reads I1 as draft; reviewer approves and locks I1; editor submits its old draft change. The server must check role, owner and current draft state at the protected update, so the edit fails after approval. Under a conditional-update design, the editor’s update includes state=draft and checks the affected-row count; approval changes draft→approved under the database’s selected transaction rules. If editing commits first, approval must deliberately approve that current version. Define version/locking policy rather than relying on the page’s old state.

W13.concept: Access control decides which actions a user can take on each object. Business rules add conditions such as ownership, subscription or workflow stage.
W13.mechanism: State the user–action–object rule, enforce it on every relevant route and verify both allowed behaviour and denied effects.
W13.example: Model an invitation flow with owner, editor, and viewer roles. Define who may invite whom and which roles may be granted. Test each permitted and forbidden transition with controlled accounts. Include a viewer directly calling the invitation endpoint, rather than assuming a hidden button prevents that action.
W13.pitfall: Checking permissions only on page rendering leaves direct API requests unprotected.

check.question: Where should the rule 'a viewer cannot grant editor access' be enforced?
choices: Only by hiding the editor option in HTML
In the server operation that creates or changes the invitation
Only in a welcome email
check.explanation: The state-changing operation must enforce the rule regardless of how the request was constructed.

guide.bridge: S03 introduced authentication tags and S04 introduced signatures. Use fictional tokens and keys from the lesson.
guide.teaching:
### Read the parts without trusting them

A common JSON Web Token has encoded header, payload and signature sections. The payload can contain claims such as issuer, subject and expiry. Encoding makes it transportable; it does not make it secret or verified.

Decoding a token is not the same as validating it. Anyone can write a payload claiming to be an administrator.

### Verify under a fixed policy

The application chooses acceptable algorithms, keys and issuers. It must not let an untrusted header freely decide how verification works. Verify the signature or MAC with the intended key and library configuration.

### Check whether the token belongs here

Validate relevant issuer, audience, time and token-purpose rules. The audience identifies the intended recipient. A valid token for another service may be inappropriate for this API.

Then enforce the current user's permissions on the requested object. A verified identity claim does not grant unlimited access.

### Consider the token's lifetime

A token can remain valid after a permission changes unless the system supplies a revocation or current-state check. Document expiry, key rotation, storage and logout behaviour. Do not put secrets in an ordinary signed JWT payload merely because it looks unreadable.
guide.example:
Verifier policy: issuer=https://issuer.example; audience=notes-api;
algorithm=selected RS256 implementation; current time=1000
A: correct signature, iss correct, aud notes-api, exp 1100 -> accept
B: same but aud other-api -> reject
C: same but exp 900       -> reject
D: modified payload with old signature -> reject
E: decoded claims only, no verification -> never treat as authenticated
guide.explanation: All claim values are fictional. The fixture avoids hand-writing a verifier: a maintained JWT library must handle signature encoding and cryptographic validation. Token acceptance is a conjunction of required checks, not a choice of whichever check succeeds.
guide.exercise: Evaluate all five cases and add a correct signature with the wrong issuer and a token requesting an unsupported algorithm. State which policy check rejects each.
guide.solution: Only A is accepted. Wrong audience, expired, modified, unverified, wrong issuer and unsupported algorithm reject for their respective reasons. A valid signature does not waive claim requirements.
guide.challenge: A token for user A is valid for notes-api and unexpired. A requests B's note. Explain both token validation and the separate object decision, including a test that distinguishes them.
guide.challenge_solution: Token validation authenticates A under the policy; ownership still denies B's note. Test A's own note as allowed and B's as denied using the same valid token. Never interpret successful JWT verification as universal data access.

W14.concept: A JWT is a token format that carries claims. Those claims become useful evidence only after the application verifies the token and checks that it is appropriate for this operation.
W14.mechanism: Decode only to inspect. Verify the allowed algorithm and key, check issuer, audience, time and purpose, then perform the normal permission decision.
W14.example: Decode a synthetic course token without treating decoding as verification. List which claims are visible. Then use the provider's supported verification library to test valid, expired, wrong-audience, and altered tokens. Document the trusted key source separately from any untrusted key identifier in the token header.
W14.pitfall: A library returning decoded JSON may not have verified authenticity. Read the API contract carefully.

check.question: Does base64url-decoding a JWT establish its authenticity?
choices: Yes; readable JSON is proof of a valid signature
Yes; a token with three parts cannot be altered
No; signature and claim validation are separate required checks
check.explanation: Decoding only interprets the representation. Verification establishes integrity under a trusted key and validation policy.

guide.bridge: S06 introduced sessions and W14 introduced token validation. Follow the supplied fictional authorisation flow on paper.
guide.teaching:
### Name the participants

The user owns or controls access to a resource. The client application asks for delegated access. An authorisation server issues the permission, and a resource server accepts a suitable access token.

An access token is a credential for a stated service and scope. Scope describes requested permissions. It is not automatically proof that the user has signed into your own application.

### Follow the redirect carefully

The browser may be redirected to the authorisation server and then back to a registered callback. Check the destination exactly under the provider's rules. A broad or incorrectly matched redirect can send sensitive flow information to the wrong place.

State helps connect a callback with the request your application began. PKCE binds a code exchange to a verifier created for that flow, reducing certain code-interception risks. Use a maintained implementation rather than assembling isolated checks from memory.

### Separate access from identity

OpenID Connect adds an identity layer with its own ID-token validation rules. Check issuer, audience and other required claims. Do not use an arbitrary access token as an interchangeable identity token.

### Minimise what you request

Ask for only the permissions needed, protect credentials and document refresh and revocation behaviour. A successful provider approval still leaves your application responsible for its own object-access checks.

### Trace the code flow

1. The client begins a flow with a random state value and PKCE verifier, sending the corresponding challenge and registered redirect information.
2. The browser visits the authorisation server, where the user signs in and reviews the requested access under that service's process.
3. The server sends an authorisation code back through the registered browser redirect.
4. The client checks its flow binding and exchanges the code with the required verifier and client authentication where applicable.
5. The client uses the resulting appropriately scoped token at its intended resource service.

The exact protocol and client type define the required checks. A code reaching the wrong callback, a wrong state or a wrong verifier should not become a successful delegated operation.
guide.example:
Invented trace
Client chooses state=S1 and verifier=V1; sends challenge derived from V1.
Browser -> authorisation server: client ID, exact redirect, state S1, challenge.
Browser -> approved callback: code C1, state S1.
Client checks state, redeems C1 with V1 under provider rules.
Resource call uses the resulting access token for its intended audience.
Wrong returned state S2 -> stop before treating flow as successful.
guide.explanation: The values are labels, not secure random implementations. A redirect carrying a code does not by itself prove success. The receiver must bind it to the initiating transaction and complete the protocol correctly. An access token intended for another API is not interchangeable.
guide.exercise: Draw the five steps and label browser versus client/server exchanges. Evaluate wrong state, wrong PKCE verifier and unregistered redirect scenarios. State where each should fail.
guide.solution: Step 1 happens inside the initiating client: create transaction state and a verifier. Step 2 navigates the browser to the authorisation server. Step 3 redirects that browser back to the registered client callback with code and state. Step 4 is the client’s code-redemption exchange with the token endpoint; a server-mediated client does this from its backend, while a supported browser client follows its provider’s architecture. Step 5 sends the resulting access token to the intended resource API. Wrong state fails client transaction validation; wrong verifier fails PKCE redemption at the authorisation server; an unregistered redirect fails provider redirect validation. Neither a browser redirect nor a decoded token alone proves a complete successful flow.
guide.challenge: Explain why an OAuth access token is not automatically an identity assertion for your application. Define one test for wrong audience and one for a callback replay or code reuse.
guide.challenge_solution: Use the protocol's intended authentication mechanism and validate its issuer/audience/context. Wrong-audience credentials reject; a consumed code cannot establish a fresh session through replay. Provider-specific error semantics should be tested in a designated environment.

W15.concept: OAuth lets an application receive limited permission to use another service. Signing a user in through an identity provider adds identity rules beyond that delegated access.
W15.mechanism: Keep client, authorisation server and resource server roles clear. Validate redirects and flow binding, distinguish access tokens from identity assertions, and request limited scope.
W15.example: Draw a modern authorisation-code flow with PKCE using a synthetic account in the course lab. Label the authorisation code, verifier, access token, and any ID token. Explain why an access token for one API is not automatically a valid login assertion for a different client. Test the lab's mismatched redirect or transaction case within scope.
W15.pitfall: Access tokens and ID tokens have different audiences and purposes. Similar-looking token formats do not make them interchangeable.

check.question: What does PKCE help bind?
choices: Authorisation-code redemption to possession of the initiating client's verifier
All API permissions to the user's display name
A password to every unrelated website
check.explanation: The code challenge and verifier connect code redemption to the initiating client instance under the flow's assumptions.

guide.bridge: C07 introduced concurrency and B02 introduced transactions. Imagine the last available seat being requested twice.
guide.teaching:
### Trace the two requests

Request A reads “one seat left”. Before A writes, request B reads the same value. Both decide a booking is allowed. If each then writes independently, two bookings may be created for one seat.

The problem is a race between checking and using shared state. Making each individual database write valid does not necessarily preserve the larger rule.

### State what must always remain true

“Bookings must not exceed capacity” is an invariant: a condition the system should preserve through every allowed change. Use ordinary words first, then express it in the database or transaction design.

### Enforce the rule where updates meet

Depending on the database and operation, a suitable transaction, row lock, conditional update or uniqueness constraint may make the decision safe. Check the actual isolation and failure behaviour. A lock in one web process may not protect requests handled by another process.

### Make duplicate requests safe too

Retries are different from competing requests but can cause the same unwanted duplicate effect. Use a suitable operation key and stored result where needed. Test deliberate interleavings with fictional data in the lab, and inspect the final bookings rather than counting success responses alone.
guide.example:
Voucher V: unused
1. Request A reads unused
2. Request B reads unused
3. A grants credit and marks used
4. B grants credit and marks used
Fault: two grants for one voucher

Repair concept: atomically claim unused V; only the successful claimant grants credit
Include claim+credit in one consistent transaction.
guide.explanation: Marking used after granting credit leaves a window. Moving the flag earlier without transaction/failure handling can instead consume the voucher without delivering credit. Both outcomes violate a complete business contract, so examine crash paths as well as concurrent success.
guide.exercise: Trace the supplied schedule and a serial order. Define the invariant and expected number of successful redemptions. Add a failure between claim and credit and state whether rollback or durable recovery is required.
guide.solution: Exactly one committed grant is permitted. Serial processing yields one success and one denial. A partial claim/credit operation needs atomic rollback or a documented durable recovery process; an in-memory flag alone is insufficient.
guide.challenge: Design request retries with keys K1 and K2 under user A. State what a repeated K1 returns, what happens when K1 is reused with a different amount and why user B cannot retrieve A's cached outcome.
guide.challenge_solution: Repeated same operation/key returns the stored outcome without another effect. Different payload under K1 rejects. Scope keys/outcomes by principal and operation, and protect their storage with the state transition. A different K2 still must obey the voucher invariant.

W16.concept: A web action may check a rule and update data in separate steps. Two requests can slip between those steps and both act on an old state.
W16.mechanism: Protect the complete read–check–update rule at the shared state boundary. Test concurrent requests and retries against the actual stored invariant.
W16.example: Model one-use redemption as unused → used. Draw two requests both observing unused, then both granting credit. Repair the local model with an atomic conditional update or an appropriate unique constraint and transaction. Test overlapping requests in the authorised lab and verify the final ledger, not just the number of successful HTTP responses.
W16.pitfall: A transaction boundary alone does not imply the isolation level needed for every invariant. State the guarantee you rely on.

check.question: What must a single-use redemption protect?
choices: Only the visual button's disabled state
The eligibility check and state change as one invariant-preserving operation
Only the time between two browser clicks
check.explanation: The server must prevent competing operations from both consuming the same entitlement.

guide.bridge: N06 introduced HTTP and proxies; N04 introduced message framing. Use only supplied traces or the dedicated isolated lab.
guide.teaching:
### Remember why framing is needed

A connection can carry more than one request. Each receiving component needs rules for the request line, headers and body length. That is framing: identifying the boundaries of one message.

### Compare the two interpretations

A front proxy may forward bytes using one interpretation while the backend parses them using another. If they disagree about a body boundary, leftover bytes can be treated as part of a later request. This family of issues is called request smuggling.

The vulnerability depends on the actual chain of parsers and protocol conversions. Seeing an unusual header alone does not prove the disagreement exists.

### Remove ambiguity

Use consistent maintained components and reject invalid or ambiguous message forms under the deployed protocol rules. Pay attention to conversion between HTTP versions and to any intermediary that rewrites headers.

### Inspect without overclaiming

For a supplied trace, mark what each parser believes the request length to be. State the observed response, the connection reuse assumptions and any missing backend evidence. In a shared live system, such experiments can affect other users, which is why this course confines them to isolated authorised targets.
guide.example:
Abstract fixture: byte positions 0..19
Front parser assumes body ends after position 9.
Back parser assumes body ends after position 14.
Bytes 10..14 are therefore interpreted differently.

Parser F: request 1=[0..9], next begins 10
Parser B: request 1=[0..14], next begins 15
Question: can both sides safely reuse this connection as if aligned?
guide.explanation: Positions are inclusive: 0..9 contains 10 bytes, while 0..14 contains 15. Parser F leaves position 10 as the next request’s start; parser B treats 10..14 as part of the first request and starts the next at 15. Thus the same five bytes have conflicting meanings. The model is not valid HTTP syntax. A status code alone does not establish this parser path.
guide.exercise: Draw both boundary views for the supplied 20-byte fixture. Then use matching end positions 9/9 and explain the difference. State two requirements for a defensive proxy/backend configuration review.
guide.solution: Draw F as [0..9] | [10..19] and B as [0..14] | [15..19]. In the 9/9 variant both start the next request at 10, so this particular boundary disagreement is absent. That does not prove the requests or implementation are otherwise safe. Review strict framing validation, consistent interpretation through each proxy/translation hop, and how ambiguous messages are rejected and connections closed rather than reused out of alignment.
guide.challenge: Write a provider-lab evidence plan identifying scope, front/back protocol assumptions, baseline, one controlled variation, expected boundary effect and a safe stop condition. Explain why success against one parser version does not prove all deployments share the fault.
guide.challenge_solution: Parsing and translation behaviour depend on actual components/configuration. Evidence must support the tested chain and avoid extrapolation. Do not send framing experiments to unrelated production sites.

W17.concept: A proxy and a backend must agree on where each HTTP request ends. If they interpret the same bytes differently, one request can affect how another is read.
W17.mechanism: Compare every relevant parser's message boundaries. A smuggling claim needs evidence of a meaningful disagreement in the deployed request chain.
W17.example: Draw a frontend-to-backend byte stream containing two harmless requests. Mark the boundary each component expects under the lab's controlled disagreement. Explain how the two interpretations diverge without testing public infrastructure. For the remediation exercise, state which component rejects ambiguity and verify the normal request path still functions.
W17.pitfall: A timeout alone is not proof of request smuggling. It may reflect many unrelated parser or network behaviours.

check.question: What is the central failure behind request smuggling?
choices: The browser uses a long password
A database table lacks an index
Intermediaries disagree about request framing boundaries
check.explanation: Different framing interpretations let bytes acquire unintended meaning across shared connections.

guide.bridge: You have studied access checks, input interpretation and request handling. Use only the specified training application and fictional accounts.
guide.teaching:
### Define the task before testing

Write the target, permitted operations, accounts, data and stopping conditions. Draw the main user journeys and identify which assets and permissions they involve.

Prioritise questions with meaningful consequences. Can a user read another user's record? Can supplied text become a database or shell instruction? Can one request perform an unintended second action?

### Keep each test tied to a rule

Record the expected behaviour, one controlled change and the actual result. Use the smallest permitted demonstration that establishes the issue. A tool's alert is a lead to investigate, not a finished finding.

### Explain the evidence

A report should identify the affected operation, prerequisites, repeatable lab steps and verified impact. Separate observed facts from possible wider consequences. Do not include unrelated credentials or other people's data.

### Verify the repair

Repeat the narrow failing case after the fix, then check the legitimate journey. Consider related entry points that share the same faulty logic. A fix that blocks the demonstration but breaks normal users or leaves another route open is incomplete.

Finish by recording coverage limits. An assessment has a scope and time window; it cannot promise that an application has no other vulnerabilities.
guide.example:
Fictional note API packet
A owns n1; B owns n2; body max 100 chars.
Observed: A GET n2 ->200 with B's body.
Observed: PATCH n1 accepts owner=B from request body.
Observed: note preview inserts body using innerHTML despite plain-text contract.
Observed: A GET n1 ->200; B GET n2 ->200.
Scope: analyse packet only; make no external requests.
guide.explanation: The first observation is object-authorisation failure, the second protected-property assignment, and the third a text/markup boundary problem. The packet supports design findings without requiring attack execution. Existing valid owner reads are essential regression cases.
guide.exercise: Write three findings from the packet. Each needs problem, exact evidence, plausible impact, root cause, minimal repair and positive/negative verification cases. Include a scope and untested-behaviour section.
guide.solution: Scope: analyse only the supplied fictional packet; no external requests were made. Untested: runtime exploitability, other endpoints, concurrency, deployment and real data. Finding 1 — cross-owner note disclosure. Evidence: A GET n2 returned 200 with B’s body although B owns n2. The intended rule is that each learner reads only their own notes. The supported impact is disclosure of that private note; the packet does not establish access to every note. Root cause: missing or ineffective object-owner enforcement on this read path. Repair: derive A from verified identity and constrain the object lookup/authorisation by owner. Recheck A/n1 and B/n2 succeed; A/n2 and B/n1 deny without bodies. Finding 2 — protected-field assignment. Evidence: PATCH n1 accepts owner=B from caller-controlled data. This can break the ownership policy; downstream effects need separate evidence. Root cause: a writable contract that includes or blindly copies a protected field. Repair: accept only the documented body field, derive owner from trusted state and reject unknown/protected keys. Recheck an ordinary permitted body update succeeds; supplied owner, wrong types and oversized bodies reject and leave ownership unchanged. Cover single and bulk update paths. Finding 3 — unsafe plain-text preview. Evidence: the preview uses innerHTML for a body whose contract is plain text. This establishes an unintended HTML-parsing boundary; it does not alone prove executable XSS under the deployed browser/policy. Repair: render body with textContent. Recheck ordinary text still displays and practice remains literal with no nested b element. Cover main, preview and export renderers rather than only one screen. A complete report keeps observed facts separate from predicted effects and records the regression result for each path.
guide.challenge: Independently review a changed packet: ownership checks are fixed, but the export preview still uses innerHTML and bulk PATCH still accepts owner. State which original findings remain, identify the alternate paths and propose a regression matrix.
guide.challenge_solution: The object-read finding can close only for verified paths. Rendering and protected-field issues remain in alternate paths. Include main/export views and single/bulk writes. A fix in the primary screen does not establish coverage of every entrypoint.

W18.concept: An application-security assessment brings earlier checks together around a defined service. A useful finding explains the broken rule, its actual effect and how to verify a fix.
W18.mechanism: Assess a defined scope, test specific rules, report observed effects and verify both the fix and legitimate use. Keep untested possibilities separate from findings.
W18.example: Assess the supplied application using an owner, a second user, and a logged-out session. Cover input handling, ownership, authentication lifecycle, cross-origin behaviour, file boundaries, and concurrent state changes. Rank findings by supported impact and likelihood. Repair at least one issue, add a regression check, and ask the other learner to reproduce the finding from the report alone.
W18.pitfall: A long tool output is not an assessment report. Explain which observed behaviour violates which rule and what evidence supports that conclusion.

check.question: What best demonstrates a finding is reproducible?
choices: Another learner can follow the scoped report and observe the same violated property
The original tester remembers the steps
The scanner lists many severity labels
check.explanation: Independent reproduction checks that the report contains sufficient evidence and instructions rather than relying on hidden knowledge.

guide.bridge: C02 covered bounds and C04 covered lifetime. Examine the supplied tiny program in the isolated lab.
guide.teaching:
### Find the invalid operation

A buffer overflow writes beyond available storage. An out-of-bounds read accesses data outside the intended object. A use-after-free accesses an object whose lifetime has ended. These mistakes have different starting points, so identify the exact operation first.

### Follow what is affected

An invalid write may damage nearby data, a pointer or information used to return from a function. An invalid read may reveal data or crash. The result depends on the layout, input, compiler and platform protections.

Do not assume every crash gives control of execution. Equally, a program continuing to run does not prove the invalid access was harmless.

### Use a causal trace

Record the input, expected boundary, offending operation and observed consequence. A debugger or suitable runtime checker can help connect them in your local teaching program. Separate the point where corruption occurred from the later point where it became visible.

### Repair the underlying rule

Fix length arithmetic, bounds or lifetime ownership as appropriate. Add meaningful boundary tests and consider safer abstractions. A layout change that makes one demonstration stop working is not the same as removing the invalid access.
guide.example:
Abstract memory (not an actual compiler layout)
index: 0 1 2 3 | adjacent object
array: A B C 0 | flag=0
capacity 4 includes terminator.
Attempt to store "ABCDE" plus terminator needs 6 bytes.
Root cause: required size 6 exceeds capacity 4.
Repair policy: reject input; do not perform a partial unsafe write.
guide.explanation: The 0 in the array is the zero-valued terminating byte, not the printable digit "0". Five ASCII letters plus that byte need 6 slots. The model makes the arithmetic visible without relying on a platform-specific layout; the neighbouring flag is illustrative, not a promise about an actual C stack. Reject before copying. If you checked only after copying, the invalid write would already have happened.
guide.exercise: For capacity 8, calculate required bytes for ASCII strings of lengths 0,7,8 and 12 with a terminator. Classify accepted/rejected inputs under a no-truncation policy. State a separate lifetime defect not captured by this capacity check.
guide.solution: Add one terminating byte: lengths 0, 7, 8 and 12 require 1, 8, 9 and 13 bytes. With capacity 8 and no truncation, accept lengths 0 and 7; reject 8 and 12 before writing. Capacity and lifetime are different: a pointer to an already freed 8-byte allocation is invalid even for a one-byte access.
guide.challenge: Write a root-cause report for a hypothetical copy of 10 bytes into an 8-byte object. Separate proven bounds failure, possible consequences and evidence still needed before claiming exploitability.
guide.challenge_solution: Proven in the model: writing 10 bytes into an 8-byte object exceeds capacity by 2, violating the bounds invariant. Possible effects include corrupted adjacent data, a crash or control-flow impact, but the packet does not prove which occurs. Needed evidence includes input reachability, actual layout, first invalid access and applicable protections. Repair the size/lifetime contract and test required sizes 7, 8 and 9: first two fit this 8-byte object, the last rejects.

F01.concept: Memory corruption means a program reads or changes memory outside the rules it should follow. The important question is how that mistake affects data or control flow.
F01.mechanism: Identify the invalid memory operation, trace its consequences under stated conditions and repair the bounds or lifetime rule that allowed it.
F01.example: Take a deliberately unsafe local buffer exercise and draw its valid range. Use a diagnostic build to identify the first invalid access. Reduce the input until the smallest reproducer remains. Replace the unsafe length assumption with an explicit capacity check, then verify both the reproducer and ordinary boundary cases.
F01.pitfall: A crash is evidence of a failure, not automatically proof of a particular exploit capability or severity.

check.question: What is the strongest first step after observing a memory-related crash?
choices: Assume arbitrary code execution has been demonstrated
Disable every diagnostic to improve speed
Find and minimise the input that causes the first invalid access
check.explanation: A minimal reproducer and diagnostic evidence support a causal explanation and a targeted repair.

guide.bridge: F01 introduced memory corruption. Compare protections against a known local example rather than assuming that a label means complete safety.
guide.teaching:
### Match each protection with its job

Address-space layout randomisation, or ASLR, varies locations to make useful addresses harder to predict. Non-executable memory aims to stop instructions being run from regions meant for data. A stack canary places a check value to detect some overwrites before returning.

These mechanisms address different exploitation steps. None automatically prevents every out-of-bounds access or incorrect program decision.

### Understand control-flow protection

Control-flow integrity restricts certain transfers of execution to permitted destinations under a policy. The strength of that policy and the operations it covers matter. A broad set of permitted targets may leave more room than a narrow one.

### Consider prevention as well as mitigation

Memory-safe languages and safe interfaces can remove classes of invalid access. Their guarantees still depend on unsafe code, foreign-library boundaries and implementation details. A language choice does not automatically fix access-control or business-logic errors.

### Interpret a changed result carefully

If a protection turns a local overwrite into a detected crash, that is a useful observed difference. Report what was blocked and under which build settings. Continue to fix the original invalid access and check normal behaviour.

In particular, a memory-safe application may call unsafe native libraries. Inspect those boundaries and their ownership rules rather than assuming the calling language automatically protects every library operation.
guide.example:
Fault: write 9 bytes into an 8-byte object.
Bounds check: rejects before write -> addresses root cause.
NX: may block execution from a data page -> write can still corrupt data.
ASLR: changes addresses -> does not make 9 fit into 8.
Canary: may detect some overwrites -> layout/path dependent.
Memory-safe container: enforces bounds under its supported operations.
guide.explanation: The key arithmetic remains wrong under all layout mitigations. Data-only corruption may matter even when injected code cannot execute. A useful report explains the remaining consequence rather than dismissing a bug because one exploit technique is harder.
guide.exercise: Create a table for all five example controls: bounds checking, NX, ASLR, canary and a memory-safe container. For each give its prevention/detection/hardening role, assumption and one remaining risk. For one selected mitigation describe how the supported lab would inspect actual build/runtime evidence, without attempting an exploit. Paper plans must be labelled unperformed.
guide.solution: Bounds check: prevents this write if every relevant path checks the true capacity before access; lifetime defects can remain. NX: hardens execution from selected pages if permissions are applied; data corruption remains. ASLR: hardens address prediction if relevant mappings are randomised and not exposed by leaks; the overflow still exists. Canary: detects selected overwrites if the protected marker is checked before return; other objects/paths can be missed. Memory-safe container: prevents unsupported out-of-bounds access under its operation guarantees; unsafe/native interfaces or logic bugs remain. Example verification plan: in the designated Linux lab inspect the target artifact’s stack-execution metadata with the provider’s documented tool and compare it with runtime page permissions. Record platform, binary and actual observations; a build flag or paper prediction alone is not runtime verification.
guide.challenge: A reviewer says “ASLR is enabled, so the overflow is fixed.” Write a precise response and propose both a source repair and a boundary regression test.
guide.challenge_solution: ASLR does not repair the out-of-bounds operation. Check required capacity before copying or use a representation that enforces bounds; test just-below, exact-fit and over-limit input while preserving ordinary successful use.

F02.concept: Memory-safety protections make some failures harder to exploit or easier to detect. Each protection has a specific job and leaves other problems to solve.
F02.mechanism: State what each mitigation blocks and what assumptions it needs. Keep repairing the underlying defect rather than treating one blocked exploit path as complete safety.
F02.example: For a provided local program, identify which hardening features are enabled using the course tooling. Draw one bug's path and annotate which layer might interrupt it and which conditions bypass that layer's scope. Repair the bug and retain the mitigation. Explain the difference between preventing an invalid write and detecting one of its consequences.
F02.pitfall: A mitigation stopping one demonstration does not prove the underlying program is memory-safe.

check.question: What does a stack canary primarily do?
choices: Detect certain stack overwrites before a protected return
Prevent all heap lifetime errors
Validate every application permission
check.explanation: A canary checks a particular integrity marker. It does not provide comprehensive bounds, lifetime, or authorisation safety.

guide.bridge: C06 introduced operating-system permissions and B04 introduced isolation. Draw a small service with a public request handler and private data.
guide.teaching:
### List the necessary actions

The public handler may need to read a request and ask for one approved operation. It may not need direct access to every database table, the host filesystem or account-management keys.

Separate the less-trusted parsing work from operations holding stronger permissions. The interface between them should accept a narrow defined request, not arbitrary instructions.

### Understand a capability

A capability is a reference or credential granting particular authority over a resource under the system's model. Possessing it can allow an operation, so protect how it is issued, passed and revoked.

A sandbox restricts a program's available resources or operations. Its value depends on actual configuration and enforcement, including filesystem, network and process access.

### Check both directions

A privileged helper must validate requests from the unprivileged component. Otherwise the helper can become a way to perform forbidden work indirectly. Also limit what sensitive results return through that interface.

### Plan for compromise

Ask what an attacker could still do if the public handler were fully controlled. That question tests the boundary more strongly than assuming the handler remains polite. The exercise's diagram should identify remaining authority and a recovery path.
guide.example:
Design fixture: document renderer
Untrusted renderer: read one supplied input; write one output directory.
Denied: network, home directory, subprocess launch.
Privileged broker: choose input/output handles; validate size and result.
Interface: render(document_id), not run(command) or read(any_path).
Expected ordinary case: render synthetic note successfully.
guide.explanation: The broker decides which object handles the renderer receives. If it passes an unrestricted directory handle or accepts arbitrary paths, the interface may leak broader access. A successful render proves functionality, while denied-access checks provide evidence for selected confinement properties.
guide.exercise: For the renderer fixture, list assets, allowed operations and five denied operations. Define one positive test and three harmless negative tests you would perform in the supported lab. Label paper expectations separately from observed results.
guide.solution: Allowed work: read the supplied synthetic document and write its result in the designated output area. Five denials: read unrelated synthetic files; write outside the output area; make network connections; launch subprocesses; request another user’s document through the broker. Positive plan: render the supplied note and check expected output. Three harmless lab checks can attempt access to a disposable unrelated file, a forbidden loopback connection, and creation outside the output area; each should be denied under the chosen policy. These remain expectations until tested in the supported lab. A denied filesystem test does not by itself verify network or broker policy.
guide.challenge: A helper runs with broad file access and exposes copy(source,destination) to an untrusted renderer. Explain how this undermines separation and redesign the interface around explicit object authority.
guide.challenge_solution: Arbitrary source/destination paths let the renderer direct privileged operations. Replace them with validated object IDs or pre-opened constrained handles, limit output destinations and enforce caller/context rules in the broker.

F03.concept: A component should receive only the authority it needs. Privilege separation divides work so a failure in one part does not automatically expose everything.
F03.mechanism: Give each part only the required authority, use a narrow checked interface between privilege levels and reason about what remains possible after a component fails.
F03.example: Design a document-conversion service with an untrusted parser and a separate storage component. Grant the parser access only to its input and output, not the whole archive or network. Draw the message interface and state which component authorises the requested file. Consider what an attacker could still do after taking control of the parser.
F03.pitfall: A sandbox with an unrestricted host filesystem mount can inherit the very authority it was meant to remove.

check.question: What makes privilege separation useful after one component is compromised?
choices: Every component runs as the same administrator
The compromised component has less authority than the whole service
The process names are different
check.explanation: Separating authority limits consequences. Process separation without permission separation may provide little containment.

guide.bridge: F03 introduced limited authority. Use the fictional host inventory and the named lab environment.
guide.teaching:
### Know what is running

Inventory the services, accounts, software versions and exposed ports. An unused service still needs maintenance if it remains reachable. Remove or disable unnecessary components under a controlled plan rather than changing an unknown host blindly.

### Restrict permitted connections

A firewall applies rules to traffic under its observation. State the source, destination, direction and service each rule permits. A host rule and a network-edge rule can see different traffic.

“Inside the network” is not a complete trust policy. Internal accounts and services still need authentication and appropriate permissions.

### Keep maintenance and recovery usable

Apply supported updates, manage administrative access and keep recoverable backups. Test that the intended service still works and that administrators retain a safe recovery route after a rule change.

### Detect with a question in mind

Intrusion detection looks for suspicious behaviour or indicators. An alert needs context: which host, which event and which rule. Normal administrative work may resemble an attack, while some attacks do not match a known signature.

Write what the control prevents, what evidence it records and what an operator should do next. A tool installed without usable configuration and response steps provides limited protection.

An IPv4 listener bound to 127.0.0.1 is ordinarily loopback-only. A listener bound to 0.0.0.0 asks to accept on all relevant local IPv4 interfaces. Actual reachability still depends on routing and network controls. That distinction explains why the fictional local-only exercise needs investigation when it appears on 0.0.0.0.
guide.example:
Fictional workstation baseline
Inbound: deny by default; no externally listening training server.
Outbound: required update/documentation services under policy.
Accounts: ordinary daily user; separate approved admin action.
Backups: versioned; weekly harmless restore check.
Logs: authentication and configuration changes with UTC/source IDs.
Alert: unexpected new listener -> investigate, not automatic proof of compromise.
guide.explanation: The baseline combines preventive and detective controls. An unexpected listener may be legitimate new software, a misconfiguration or malicious activity. Investigation should establish process identity, binding and change context before assigning intent.
guide.exercise: Create a baseline for a fictional training laptop. For each item give desired state, observation method, owner and rollback/recovery step. Analyse a synthetic alert: process demo-server listening on 0.0.0.0:8765 after a local-only exercise.
guide.solution: Example rows for the fictional training laptop: (1) Training server is loopback-only; observe its documented bind address; learner owns the configuration; stop it or restore the prior loopback setting on failure. (2) Required updates remain reachable; use the platform’s normal update status rather than arbitrary scanning; device owner maintains it; roll back the scoped rule if the approved update check fails. (3) Backup can restore a disposable marker; record the actual restore result; device owner maintains copies; retain the previous known-good backup if the new check fails. For demo-server on 0.0.0.0:8765, 0.0.0.0 means all IPv4 interfaces rather than loopback only, so the bind differs from the exercise intention. Verify process identity and configuration, stop/reconfigure that training service and retest. The alert does not prove an intruder, and IPv6 exposure needs a separate check.
guide.challenge: A firewall change blocks updates and remote recovery. Explain the availability impact and write a safer rollout plan with baseline capture, one scoped change, positive/negative checks and rollback criteria.
guide.challenge_solution: Use a reversible controlled change, verify required legitimate paths and blocked unwanted paths, retain a recovery route and roll back when stated checks fail. A control is not successful merely because it blocks more traffic.

F04.concept: Hardening reduces unnecessary ways into a system. Network controls restrict connections, and detection records signs that something may be wrong.
F04.mechanism: Reduce unnecessary services and authority, define allowed connections, maintain recovery and make alerts understandable enough for an operator to act on.
F04.example: For a disposable server, list listening services and define the minimum connections needed. Apply a narrow lab firewall policy, confirm the intended client still works, and verify an unwanted connection fails. Record the configuration before and after, the test source, and a recovery method in case management access is blocked.
F04.pitfall: A detector's silence is not proof that no incident occurred. It may lack the necessary visibility or rule.

check.question: What should accompany a new deny rule?
choices: Only a screenshot of the rule's name
Removal of every recovery mechanism
Tests of both the intended blocked path and required allowed paths
check.explanation: A useful control must block the threat while preserving required operation and recoverability.

guide.bridge: L03 introduced version control and P06 introduced dependencies. Use a fictional repository and harmless placeholder secrets.
guide.teaching:
### Find the inputs to the build

List source repositories, dependency versions, package sources, build tools and deployment steps. A supply-chain problem can enter before the application runs, such as a replaced package or a compromised build credential.

### Review changes where they enter

Use code review, suitable automated checks and controlled dependency updates. A lockfile records selected dependency versions; it does not prove that every selected package is safe. Check provenance and known issues appropriate to the package's role.

### Keep secrets out of ordinary artifacts

A secret grants access, such as an API key. Store it through the deployment's protected mechanism, grant limited permissions and avoid printing it in logs. If exposed, rotate or revoke it; deleting its visible line from the latest file may leave copies in history.

### Protect the release path

Limit who and what can modify workflows, approve releases and deploy to production. Build artifacts should be connected with a reviewed source version. Check that tests and build steps do not unexpectedly contact paid or sensitive services.

### Make failures actionable

Document what to do if a dependency or credential is compromised. Identify affected versions and services, replace the compromised input and verify the resulting release. A security scanner's success result is one source of evidence, not a complete development process.
guide.example:
Synthetic inventory
app -> parser-lib 1.2 -> text-core 3.0
Advisory: parser-lib versions below 1.3 mishandle oversized records.
App accepts untrusted records through parser-lib.
Plan: reproduce with harmless fixture; update to fixed supported version;
verify normal/oversized cases; record lockfile and artifact source.
No real package names or model calls are involved.
guide.explanation: The dependency is reachable from the app's input path, so the advisory is relevant under the fixture. A version comparison alone does not prove exploitability, but the observed call path strengthens the prioritisation. Record any temporary size limit and its residual risk.
guide.exercise: Create an inventory and triage note for the supplied graph. Add a fictional leaked read/write deployment token in an old commit. State immediate containment and longer-term history/build-log actions without using a real token.
guide.solution: Inventory: application directly uses parser-lib 1.2; parser-lib uses text-core 3.0 transitively. The advisory affects parser-lib below 1.3 and this app sends untrusted records through it, so the path is relevant. Propose the supported fixed version, normal/oversize regression cases and a release record; no real advisory or runtime reproduction is supplied. For the fictional leaked deployment token: immediately revoke/rotate it at the issuer, review possible use, update authorised consumers and reduce replacement permissions. Remove exposed copies from source/history/logs through the project’s approved process, knowing earlier clones can persist. Deleting the latest line alone leaves the old token’s authority intact unless revoked.
guide.challenge: A build uses a lockfile but downloads a tool from an unpinned script URL. Explain the uncovered dependency and propose a verifiable release record covering source, tool version, inputs and output artifact.
guide.challenge_solution: The build tool is part of the supply chain even if absent from application dependency files. Pin/verify its source and version, isolate credentials and record artifact provenance with repeatable checks.

F05.concept: Software depends on code, packages, build tools and credentials. Secure development checks those connections throughout the project, not only in the final application.
F05.mechanism: Track source, dependencies, credentials and build authority. Review their changes, limit permissions and connect each release with its actual inputs.
F05.example: Review a tiny sample project. Identify direct and transitive dependencies, the release entry point, and where credentials would enter. Replace a synthetic hardcoded credential with a documented secret-injection mechanism and a harmless example configuration. Add a checklist covering dependency updates, code review, release verification, and credential rotation.
F05.pitfall: Removing a leaked secret from the latest file does not invalidate copies in history, logs, or caches.

check.question: What is the required response to an actually exposed live credential?
choices: Revoke or rotate it through the issuing system and investigate its use
Only rename the variable
Only delete the newest source-code line
check.explanation: The authority must be invalidated. Editing one copy does not erase already exposed copies or prevent their use.

guide.bridge: You know processes and access controls. Use fictional evidence or the designated Windows lab, not another person's device.
guide.teaching:
### Identify the system and the account

Record the machine, relevant time reference and the account under which an action ran. A local account and a domain account have different administrative contexts. An elevated process may have more authority than an ordinary process from the same user.

### Inspect objects, not only printed text

PowerShell commands commonly pass structured objects through a pipeline. A displayed table shows selected properties, not necessarily everything in the object. Check property names and types before filtering or exporting evidence.

### Read event records in context

An event identifier has meaning within its provider and log. Check timestamp, host, account, result and logging configuration. A missing event might reflect collection settings or retention, not proof that an action never occurred.

### Preserve before changing

Prefer read-only inspection for investigation. Record the command, relevant permissions and output source. Actions such as stopping a service or clearing a log change evidence and require an appropriate response plan.

The goal is to connect observations into a supported explanation, while keeping uncertain account attribution and missing records visible.
guide.example:
# PowerShell synthetic objects; no system logs read
$events = @(
  [pscustomobject]@{Id=1;User='A';Result='Fail'},
  [pscustomobject]@{Id=2;User='A';Result='OK'},
  [pscustomobject]@{Id=3;User='B';Result='Fail'}
)
$events | Where-Object Result -eq 'Fail' | Select-Object Id,User
# Expected records: 1/A and 3/B
guide.explanation: The query filters the Result property, then projects Id and User. It does not search a rendered text table for a substring. On a non-Windows machine without PowerShell, manually apply the same predicates and label the runtime check unperformed.
guide.exercise: Run or hand-trace the supplied objects. Filter failed events for user A only, then count failures by user. Record input records and expected output separately from any optional host observations.
guide.solution:
The A-only failure is Id 1. Add these lines after the supplied $events array if PowerShell is available; otherwise trace the same conditions on paper.

```powershell
$events | Where-Object { $_.Result -eq 'Fail' -and $_.User -eq 'A' } | Select-Object Id,User
$events | Where-Object Result -eq 'Fail' | Group-Object User | Select-Object Name,Count
```

Inside the braces, $_ means the current object and -and requires both conditions. Group-Object collects matching User values; the groups are A with Count 1 and B with Count 1. These are synthetic counts, not findings about an actual endpoint.
guide.challenge: Explain what additional metadata a real event record needs for an investigation: provider/source, time/offset, host, collection provenance and field schema. Give one reason a missing event might not prove the activity never occurred.
guide.challenge_solution: Logging can be disabled, filtered, rotated or uncollected. Event meaning requires source/schema and time context. A sound answer distinguishes missing visibility from evidence of absence.

D01.concept: Windows security investigation starts with understanding accounts, services, files and recorded events. PowerShell helps inspect them, but each command should answer a specific question.
D01.mechanism: Identify host, account and time context; inspect the actual PowerShell properties and event provider; preserve evidence before taking state-changing action.
D01.example: In a disposable Windows lab, enumerate a harmless directory's ACL and inspect a known service's configured account. Generate a benign test event using the course exercise and locate it in the relevant log. Export the event with context, then explain what it directly shows and what it cannot prove about the actor's intent.
D01.pitfall: An event identifier has meaning within its provider and context. A number alone is insufficient evidence.

check.question: What is distinctive about a normal PowerShell pipeline?
choices: It can pass structured objects with properties
It can pass only raw pixels
It automatically grants administrator access
check.explanation: PowerShell commonly passes objects. This supports property-based inspection but does not remove permission requirements.

guide.bridge: S06 introduced authentication and authorisation. Use the fictional domain diagram and supplied authentication trace.
guide.teaching:
### Understand the directory's role

A directory stores information about accounts, groups and resources. Active Directory provides such services in many Windows environments. A domain controller handles important directory and authentication functions, so its authority is especially sensitive.

### Follow a Kerberos ticket

Kerberos uses tickets to help a client access a named service without sending the user's password to that service each time. The exchange depends on keys, service identities and time-related rules. A ticket is a credential with a defined purpose, not a universal permission slip.

NTLM is a different authentication mechanism used in some environments. Its challenge-response behaviour and relay risks differ from Kerberos. Identify the protocol in the supplied trace before reasoning about its guarantees.

### Trace privilege relationships

Group membership, delegated administration and service accounts can connect privileges. Draw which account can manage which object and through which mechanism. A low-privilege entry can become significant if a chain of delegated permissions reaches a sensitive service.

### Keep the conclusion specific

A log mentioning an account does not always prove the human owner performed the action. Consider service use, stolen credentials and the event's actual meaning. Limit practice to the isolated domain lab and document the observed trust relationship rather than assuming every domain has the same configuration.
guide.example:
Invented domain EXAMPLE
User A -> authentication authority -> ticket-granting ticket
A -> ticket service -> ticket for files.example
A -> file service: presents service ticket
File service -> checks A's permissions on requested folder
A belongs Readers; B belongs Editors.
Policy: Readers read; Editors read/write.
guide.explanation: The final permission check remains necessary after authentication. A Kerberos ticket is not the same object as a Windows access token attached to a process/thread. Confusing them can lead to incorrect telemetry and detection claims.
guide.exercise: Draw the exchange and evaluate A read/write and B read/write for the stated folder. Add a resource not covered by the folder policy and explain why membership alone is insufficient to infer access there.
guide.solution: A may read but not write; B may do both. Other resources need their own policy. The diagram must identify authority, client and service rather than treating every message as a password exchange.
guide.challenge: Compare a Kerberos service ticket, an NTLM challenge-response exchange and a Windows process access token at the level of purpose and observation source. State one assumption you would verify before interpreting a log as successful service access.
guide.challenge_solution: Tickets support protocol authentication; NTLM is a distinct authentication mechanism; access tokens describe local security context. Authentication success need not mean a particular object operation succeeded. Correlate service/object authorisation evidence and source-specific event meanings.

D02.concept: Enterprise identity connects users, devices and services across an organisation. A successful sign-in to one service does not mean every later action should be permitted.
D02.mechanism: Follow the actual authentication protocol and the later permission chain. Protect domain and service credentials, and interpret account events within their context.
D02.example: Using a contained course environment or saved traces, draw a user obtaining a service ticket and accessing a domain service. Mark where long-term secrets and tickets are used. Inventory a synthetic administrative role and identify which systems it can control. Compare the intended access with the actual group and delegation configuration.
D02.pitfall: A domain-joined machine is not automatically trusted for every action, and a valid ticket does not replace the service's authorisation checks.

check.question: What is the role of a Kerberos service ticket?
choices: Encrypt every file on the workstation automatically
Support authentication to a particular service under the protocol's trust relationships
Replace all object-level permissions
check.explanation: A ticket supports authentication for a service. The service must still enforce what the authenticated actor may do.

guide.bridge: B04 introduced virtual machines and S06 introduced permission. Use the fictional cloud account diagram rather than creating live resources.
guide.teaching:
### Divide the responsibilities

The provider and customer share responsibilities differently for virtual machines, managed databases and application platforms. For a virtual machine, you may manage the guest operating system. A managed database moves some maintenance to the provider while leaving your data-access configuration with you.

Read the chosen service's actual responsibility description. “In the cloud” is not a complete security design.

### Identify every credential

Identity and access management, or IAM, controls which users and workloads may do what. A workload is a running service or job, not necessarily a person. Prefer appropriately scoped short-lived identity mechanisms where available instead of copying broad permanent keys into code.

### Keep private data private

Check storage exposure, network access and object permissions separately. A private network does not make an overly powerful application identity harmless. An encrypted object can still be readable by an unintended account with the key permissions.

### Prepare for change and recovery

Record configuration changes, administrative actions and billing/resource limits. Plan how to revoke access and recover data. Verify the intended denied cases using fictional diagrams or the approved lab; do not infer security solely from a console's green status indicator.
guide.example:
Provider-neutral teaching policy
Workload W may read bucket training-notes objects under prefix public/.
W may not write objects or read private/.
Assume this policy is the sole grant; default deny.
W read public/intro.txt -> allow
W read private/note.txt -> deny
W write public/new.txt -> deny
guide.explanation: The sole-grant assumption makes the fixture determinate. A real account may inherit another grant, so effective access must include all applicable policy.
